facts.text: The Eastern Curlew is probably the world's largest sandpiper, at 60–66 cm in length and 110 cm across the wings.
facts.quote: It is not only the largest curlew but probably the world's largest sandpiper, at 60–66 cm (24–26 in) in length and 110 cm (43 in) across the wings.

facts.text: The Eastern Curlew has an extremely long bill, at 12.8–20.1 cm, rivaling the longest bill for a sandpiper.
facts.quote: The extremely long bill, at 12.8–20.1 cm (5.0–7.9 in) in length, rivals the bill size of the closely related long-billed curlew as the longest bill for a sandpiper.

facts.text: It is mostly brown, and its plain, unpatterned brown underwing and brown rump distinguish it from other curlews.
facts.quote: It is mostly brown, differentiated from other curlews by its plain, unpatterned brown underwing, and brown rump.

facts.text: The Eastern Curlew eats insects such as beetle and fly larvae on its breeding grounds, and also feeds on berries during migration.
facts.quote: On its breeding grounds the Far Eastern curlew consumes insects, such as larvae of beetles and flies, and amphipods. During migration it also feeds on berries.

facts.text: In the non-breeding season it prefers crabs and small molluscs, but also takes other crustaceans and polychaetes.
facts.quote: In the non-breeding season, it consumes marine invertebrates, preferring crabs and small molluscs but also taking other crustaceans and polychaetes.

facts.text: The Eastern Curlew breeds in northeastern Asia, from Siberia to Kamchatka, and in Mongolia.
facts.quote: The Far Eastern curlew spends its breeding season in northeastern Asia, including Siberia to Kamchatka, and Mongolia.

facts.text: The Eastern Curlew probes for invertebrates in mud with its long, decurved bill, and generally congregates in large flocks to migrate or roost.
facts.quote: It uses its long, decurved bill to probe for invertebrates in the mud. It may feed in solitary but it generally congregates in large flocks to migrate or roost.

facts.text: Its call is a sharp, clear whistle, cuuue-reee, often repeated.
facts.quote: Its call is a sharp, clear whistle, cuuue-reee, often repeated.

facts.text: As of 2024 there are an estimated 20,000 – 35,000 mature individuals, and the species is classified as Endangered.
facts.quote: As of 2024, there are an estimated 20,000 – 35,000 mature individuals in the world.
